title: The stall is not a problem
summary: When a brisket or pork shoulder gets stuck around 160°F for hours, don't panic. The meat is just sweating. Wrap it if you're in a hurry, or wait it out for better bark.

body.text: Every long cook hits a wall somewhere between 150 and 170 degrees. The meat sweats, and that sweat cools it down, same as you on a hot day. It's normal, and it passes.

body.heading: Wrap when you need to, not because you're scared
body.text: Butcher paper lets some steam out so the bark stays firm. Foil works faster but softens the bark. You don't have to wrap at all. If the bark looks dark and dinner can wait, just let it ride.

body.heading: What the stall isn't
body.text: It isn't the fat melting. The tough, chewy stuff inside the meat doesn't even start breaking down until closer to 180 or 200. The stall is just moisture sitting on the surface.

takeaways: A big brisket or pork butt can stall for 2 to 4 hours.
Only wrap after the bark is dark and set, and only if you're short on time.
Paper keeps the bark firm. Foil softens it. Pick the one you want.

title: Bark is a crust you earn
summary: Bark is the dark, tasty crust on smoked meat: dried rub, melted fat, and smoke. If it wipes off when you touch it, it wasn't done yet.

body.heading: What bark actually is
body.text: Rub dries on the surface, salt and spices toast, fat renders up through it, and smoke sticks to all of it. That dries down into a dark crust, and it takes time. It can't be rushed.

body.heading: How to get it
body.text: Put the meat on with a dry surface, leave the lid shut, and don't wrap or spritz until the rub feels dry and stuck on and looks like dark leather. Wrap too early and you'll unwrap soggy seasoning instead of bark.

body.heading: If it won't set
body.text: Leave it unwrapped and let it ride. Check your pit temp is really where you think it is, and quit peeking. Every look lets heat and smoke out.

takeaways: Don't wrap until the bark is dark and set. Ever.
Dry surface going on, lid shut, patience.
If it wipes off, it wasn't done yet.

title: Thin blue smoke or go home
summary: Thick white smoke means your wood isn't burning clean. Feed the fire small pieces of wood, often, and keep a flame going.

body.heading: Why it goes thick
body.text: Wood smoldering instead of burning. Too big a chunk, wood that isn't dry, or the fire choked down for air.

body.heading: How to fix it
body.text: Bottom dampers wide open, work the heat with the top vent. Small dry splits, added often, with a flame you can see. If the smoke goes thick mid-cook, open it up and let it burn clean again before you worry about anything else.

body.heading: When to put the meat on
body.text: Wait till the smoke turns thin and blue, so thin you can barely see it. That's the fire telling you it's ready.

takeaways: If folks down the street can see your smoke, it's too thick.
Small dry splits, often, with a flame showing.
Wait for thin blue smoke before the meat goes on.

title: Temperature is a rumor
summary: 203°F is a guess, not a rule. The meat is done when a probe slides in easy.

body.text: Stick a probe or thermometer into the flat part of the brisket. If you have to push, it ain't done. If it slides in like warm butter, pull it off.

takeaways: Start checking around 195°F.

title: Resting is still cooking
summary: Cut a brisket the minute it's done and all the juice runs out. Let it rest and it stays juicy.

body.text: Leave it whole, don't slice yet. Put it in a dry cooler or a 150°F oven for at least an hour. Two to four hours is even better.

Why rest it? Because the juice needs time to settle back through the meat. Cut it the minute it's done and all the juice runs out on the board. Give it time and the fibers relax, the juice redistributes, and the meat stays juicy when you slice.

takeaways: Rest it longer than you think you need to.

title: Match the wood to the animal
summary: Post oak for beef, hickory for pork, fruitwood for chicken and turkey. Go easy on mesquite. A little goes a long way.

body.text: A chunk of mesquite on a quick steak cook tastes great. But twelve hours of mesquite will overpower everything on the pit.

body.heading: The chart — wood, flavor, best match
body.text: Strongest to lightest. Match the wood's weight to the meat.

body.heading: Mesquite — earthy, intense, sharp
body.text: Best with: beef, short cooks and steaks. Go easy — long and low turns bitter.

body.heading: Hickory — savory, hearty, tastes the way bacon smells
body.text: Best with: pork (butts, ribs, hams), chicken, beef.

body.heading: Oak — mellow, clean, burns long and steady
body.text: Best with: brisket, beef, pork. Post oak for beef.

body.heading: Pecan — hickory's gentler cousin, sweeter and nuttier
body.text: Best with: pork, poultry, brisket.

body.heading: Maple — mild with a light sweetness
body.text: Best with: ham, poultry, cheese, vegetables.

body.heading: Cherry — sweet, fruity, paints a deep red mahogany color
body.text: Best with: poultry, pork, ham.

body.heading: Apple — sweet, delicate, the gentlest of the fruitwoods
body.text: Best with: pork, poultry, ribs, fish.

body.heading: Peach — light, sweet fruit smoke
body.text: Best with: poultry, pork.

body.heading: Alder — the most delicate smoke, barely there
body.text: Best with: salmon, fish.

takeaways: Use dry, seasoned wood. Never green wood.

title: Fat cap up, down, or does it matter?
summary: Put the fat cap toward the heat so it shields the meat. But fat doesn't drip down through the meat and baste it, no matter what folks say.

body.text: On an offset smoker, point the thick end toward the firebox. The fat protects the meat from the heat. That's all it does.

takeaways: Trim the fat to about a quarter of an inch. But be sure not to remove all the fat.

title: Spritz, mop, or leave it alone
summary: Most folks spray their meat way too much.

body.heading: What spritzing is for
body.text: A light mist keeps the surface damp so smoke sticks and color builds, and it cools any hot spots. It's a help, not a bath.

body.heading: Mop is the heavier cousin
body.text: A mop lays on more liquid, old school style. It can wash the bark right off if you mop too soon or too heavy.

body.heading: The rule
body.text: Leave it completely alone the first 3 to 4 hours until the bark sets. After that, a light mist every 20 to 30 minutes is plenty, especially when you're spraying cherry Dr Pepper and brown sugar. And leaving it alone the whole cook is a fine choice too.

takeaways: Don't spray so much you wash the crust off.
Nothing for the first 3 to 4 hours, until the bark sets.
A light mist every 20 to 30 minutes, especially with cherry Dr Pepper and brown sugar.

title: Salt early, sugar late
summary: Salting the meat the night before is the easiest way to make it taste better, and it costs nothing.

body.text: Salt it the night before if you can. Save anything sugary for a glaze near the end. Sugar burns over a long cook.

takeaways: Salt the night before. Free flavor.

title: What the circuit doesn't tell you
summary: Competition barbecue is one fancy bite for judges. Backyard barbecue is dinner for people you love.

body.text: Take the good ideas from the competition cooks and leave the rest. Burn your wood clean so the smoke stays thin, not thick and white. Rest the meat for real. And be patient with the bark, let it turn dark before you wrap. Skip the injections and the fancy tricks unless you enjoy doing them.

takeaways: You're feeding a table, not chasing a scorecard.

title: Wrap like you mean it
summary: Foil, butcher paper, or nothing — each one cooks a different brisket.

body.text: Foil (the Texas crutch) powers through the stall fastest and keeps everything juicy, but it steams the bark soft. Butcher paper breathes — the bark stays firm and the cook just slows down a little instead of stopping. No wrap at all gives you the best bark on the planet and the longest cook of your life.

Wrap when the bark is set — it shouldn't smear when you scratch it, usually around 160–170°F. For brisket, paper is the sweet spot. For pork butt, foil is fine since you're pulling it anyway. The foil boat (foil just under the bottom, top exposed) splits the difference: it protects the bottom from drying while the bark up top stays crisp.

takeaways: Match the wrap to the meat — paper for brisket, foil for pork butt, boat when you can't decide.

title: Reheat it like you cooked it
summary: Leftover brisket shouldn't eat like shoe leather.

body.text: The microwave is the enemy — it nukes the moisture right out. For sliced brisket or pulled pork, vacuum-seal or zip-bag the leftovers with a splash of beef broth or apple juice, then warm them in simmering water until they're hot through. Tastes like it just came off the pit.

Ribs go back on the smoker or in a 250°F oven, wrapped in foil with a little butter and honey, until they're hot — about 30–45 minutes. Whole turkey or chicken? Low oven (275°F), covered, with broth in the pan.

takeaways: Low and slow on the reheat, just like the cook — and always add a little liquid back.

title: Inject for insurance
summary: Brine works from the outside in. Injection puts the moisture where you need it, right now.

body.text: A good injection does two things: carries moisture deep into the meat and seasons from the inside out. It's faster than brining — no overnight wait — and you control exactly where it goes. That's why I reach for the injector over the brine bucket most days. But it's the pitmaster's call: brining still wins for whole birds and anything going in a bucket anyway.

Keep it simple: melted butter and broth for poultry, beef broth with a little Worcestershire for brisket. Inject in a grid pattern about an inch apart, going with the grain, and don't overdo it — the meat should look plump, not swollen. Wipe the surface before it hits the rub so the outside still takes seasoning.
Warm the liquid first. Cold injection into meat just off the fridge tightens everything up and the flavor doesn't spread as well.

takeaways: Injection is the fastest way to guarantee juicy meat — warm liquid, grid pattern, don't flood it.

title: A good thermometer changes the way you cook
summary: Stop cooking to time and start cooking to temperature. A leave-in probe watches the meat while you live your life; an instant-read tells the truth in seconds.

body.text: Time lies. Every brisket, butt, and bird cooks different — the thermometer doesn't guess, it knows. Cook to the number, not the clock, and a good thermometer comes in handy in ways that change a lot about the way you cook.

body.heading: Leave a probe in and live your life
body.text: A leave-in probe like an Inkbird sits in the meat the whole cook and beams the temp to your phone. No more opening the lid and dumping heat just to check.

body.heading: Settle it in two seconds
body.text: An instant-read like a ThermoWorks Thermapen ends arguments fast — spot-check five places on a brisket and know exactly where it stands.

takeaways: If you're not temping, you're guessing.
A good thermometer improves your barbecue more than any fancy gadget.

title: The smoke ring is a magic trick
summary: That pink ring under the bark isn't smoke soaking in — it's chemistry. Here's what's actually happening, and how to get a better one.

body.text: Let's get the big myth out of the way first: the smoke ring is not smoke penetrating the meat. Smoke flavor barely gets past the surface. That pink band under the bark — usually an eighth to a half inch deep — is chemistry, not soak.

When wood burns, it gives off gases including nitrogen dioxide. That gas dissolves into the moist surface of the meat and grabs onto myoglobin, the protein that makes raw meat look red-purple. The two lock together into a pink compound that heat can't brown the way the rest of the meat browns.
Here's the kicker: it's the exact same reaction as curing salt. The pink in your brisket ring and the pink in a slice of ham are cousins. You've basically got a thin cured layer under the bark.

The ring stops growing once the meat's surface passes about 140°F, because heat wrecks the myoglobin's ability to grab the gas. That's why cold meat straight from the fridge gets a better ring — it spends more time under 140°, soaking up gas before the window closes.

Want a deeper ring? Three things matter. Cold meat going on. A moist surface in the first few hours — spritzing isn't just for bark. And a clean-burning fire with good airflow, because smoldering, choked fires make less of the gas you need. Thin blue smoke, like we talked about.

And here's the part that'll start arguments: the ring means nothing about flavor. You can fake a ring in your kitchen oven with a pinch of curing salt and zero smoke. Competition judges know this — they don't score the ring. A brisket with no ring can be smokier than one with a half-inch band.

So chase the ring for the look — there's nothing wrong with pretty meat. Just don't confuse pretty with smoky, and don't trust pink to tell you it's undercooked. That ring stays pink at 203°F all day long.

takeaways: The smoke ring is nitrogen dioxide binding to myoglobin — the same chemistry as curing ham, not smoke soaking in.
Cold meat, a moist surface, and a clean fire give you the deepest ring.
The ring is cosmetic. It doesn't mean smoky, and pink doesn't mean undercooked.

title: Wrap when the color is right
summary: Once you get the dark red mahogany color you like, that is the time to wrap. Let it carry on and it will go black. A lot of people cook by color, not by time.

body.text: Here is the thing most beginners miss: you do not wrap by time. You wrap by color. Once the bark hits that dark red mahogany you are after, that is the moment. Wrap it then.
If you let it carry on past that color, it keeps darkening until it goes black. There is no coming back from black. The wrap stops the color where you want it and lets the meat finish tender inside.
A lot of experienced pitmasters cook by color, not by the clock. Learn what mahogany looks like coming off your pit and you will never over-darken a cook again.

title: Wood, strongest to lightest
summary: Smoke is an ingredient, and it comes in strengths. Mesquite will bury a chicken and hickory can bite back; alder barely whispers. The ladder, heavy at the top.

body.text: Every wood smokes different, and the difference is strength. Match the wood's weight to the meat's — a heavy wood on a long beef cook is a fine thing, but that same wood will stomp all over a fish. Here's the ladder, strongest first.

body.heading: Mesquite — the heavyweight
body.text: Earthy, intense, sharp. The strongest smoke there is. Beef loves it in short cooks and on the grill; run it long and low and it turns bitter. A little goes a long way.

body.heading: Hickory — strong
body.text: Savory and hearty, tastes the way bacon smells. The Southern standard for pork butts, ribs, and hams. Keep a heavy hand off it — too much hickory bites back with a bitter edge.

body.heading: Oak — medium-strong
body.text: Mellow and clean, and it doesn't boss the meat around. The brisket workhorse: burns long and steady, and blends with anything you pair it with.

body.heading: Pecan — medium
body.text: Hickory's gentler cousin — same family, sweeter and nuttier about it. Does right by near everything; pork and poultry shine on it.

body.heading: Maple — medium-mild
body.text: Mild with a light sweetness to it. Hams, poultry, cheese, and vegetables take to maple kindly.

body.heading: Cherry — mild
body.text: Sweet and fruity, and famous for the deep red mahogany color it paints on skin. Poultry, pork, and ham — it's the wood behind a cherry-red turkey.

body.heading: Apple — mild
body.text: Sweet and delicate, the gentlest of the common fruitwoods. Pork, poultry, and ribs; easy enough not to swamp a fish.

body.heading: Peach — mild-light
body.text: Light, sweet fruit smoke. Poultry and pork when you want just a whisper of it.

body.heading: Alder — the lightest
body.text: The most delicate smoke on the list, barely there. Born for salmon and fish — the Pacific Northwest standard.

body.heading: Putting the ladder to work
body.text: When in doubt, blend. A mellow base like oak with a few chunks of hickory or cherry over the top is how a lot of good pits run — strength where you want it, color and sweetness where you need it.

takeaways: Strongest to lightest: mesquite, hickory, oak, pecan, maple, cherry, apple, peach, alder
Heavy woods for beef and long cooks; fruitwoods for poultry, pork, and color
Blend a mild base with a stronger wood to tune the smoke to the meat

title: Stalled With Company Coming? Wrap It and Bump the Heat
summary: If the meat is stuck in the stall and your people are eating at a set time, wrap it and bump the heat. It costs you nothing in flavor — the smoke goes in early, and the rest is just getting tender.

body.text: The stall is no time to be a purist. If the meat is stuck and your people are eating at a set time, wrap it and bump the heat — the clock dictates whether you eat on time, and feeding your people on time IS barbecue.

It costs you nothing in flavor: the meat takes its smoke early — they say up to about 120 degrees — and everything after that is breaking down tissue and getting tender. Sometimes you just have to use a crutch. That's what it's for.

takeaways: The clock dictates whether you eat on time.
Meat takes its smoke early — up to about 120 degrees. After that, it's all tenderness.
Sometimes you just have to use a crutch. That's what it's for.

title: Poultry Takes Smoke Fast — Like Cheese
summary: Poultry absorbs smoke quicker than anything, just like cheese. Smoke your birds with a lighter hand — a little smoke on poultry goes a long way.

body.text: Poultry absorbs smoke quicker than anything, just like cheese. What beef takes hours to drink in, chicken grabs in no time at all.
Smoke your birds with a lighter hand — a little smoke on poultry goes a long way, and too much turns it from kissed to campfire.

takeaways: Poultry takes smoke fast — like cheese.
A little smoke on poultry goes a long way.
Too much turns it from kissed to campfire.

title: If It Makes You Happy, It's Good Barbecue
summary: Post your cook proud. If you're satisfied with the way it tastes and the way it looks, don't pay much attention to what anybody's got to say about your cook — as long as it makes you happy, that's what barbecue is all about.

body.text: Post your cook proud. People will post pictures of their food in groups and there's always somebody ready to make fun of how it looks. Here's the rule: if you're satisfied with the way it tastes and the way it looks, don't pay much attention to what anybody's got to say about your cook.
As long as it makes you happy, that's what barbecue is all about. If we all cooked the same way with the same flavor profiles, this would be a boring world.

takeaways: If you're satisfied with the way it tastes and the way it looks, don't pay much attention to what anybody's got to say about your cook.
As long as it makes you happy, that's what barbecue is all about.
If we all cooked the same way with the same flavor profiles, this would be a boring world.

title: The 10 BBQ Commandments
summary: Ten rules for the pit, written in stone and laughed at ever since. Rub thy meat, never boil a rib, and BBQ through rain, snow, sleet, or shine.

body.text: Every pit has its rules, and these ten have been passed around cookouts longer than most of us have been cooking. They read like jokes because half of them started as somebody's hard lesson.

1. Thou shall rub thy meat. 2. Thou shall not boil ribs. 3. Thou shall not use liquid smoke. 4. Thou shall not use lighter fluid. 5. Thou shall not cut meat open to inspect. 6. Thou shall not open another man's BBQ. 7. Thou shall not bad mouth fellow pitmasters. 8. Thou shall not BBQ without a drink. 9. Thou shall not open the BBQ every 5 minutes. 10. Thou shall BBQ during rain, snow, sleet or shine.
Kelly's note on number 3, in his own words from the pit: he's not using liquid smoke — it goes on the smoker. Real smoke, not a bottle.

takeaways: Rub thy meat.
Never boil a rib.
Real smoke, not a bottle.
BBQ through rain, snow, sleet, or shine.

title: The Snake Method for a Weber Kettle
summary: No fancy smoker needed. A ring of charcoal, a few wood chunks, and your Weber kettle will hold low and slow for hours — with the vents run Kelly's way.

body.text: You don't need a fancy smoker. A plain Weber kettle and a ring of charcoal will hold low and slow for hours, and the kettle you already own makes beautiful barbecue.

Line unlit briquettes around the outer edge of the charcoal grate in a C-shape, two wide and two high, and leave a gap at the end — the snake must never meet itself. Lay 3 to 5 wood chunks on top of the first third of the snake, spaced out, because the smoke goes in early. Set a water pan in the middle of the ring if you like one. Light 8 to 12 briquettes in a chimney — never lighter fluid — and set them at the head of the snake.

Kelly's vent way: bottom dampers all the way open, always. You adjust your heat with the top vent — close it down a touch to cool it off, open it up to let it run hotter. Air comes in through the bottom dampers, feeds the lit end of the snake, and leaves out the top vent. That's why the top vent sits over the meat, away from the fire: the draft pulls the heat and smoke across the food on its way out.
The meat goes on the grate opposite the lit end, indirect, and the fire eats its way around the ring on its own. Hold 225 to 250°F, and a full ring on a 22-inch kettle will run you 8 to 12 hours.

takeaways: Two wide, two high, and never let the snake meet itself.
Bottom dampers wide open; adjust heat with the top vent.
Top vent over the meat, so smoke pulls across it.
A plain Weber kettle holds low and slow for hours.

title: Keeping a Kettle Where You Want It
summary: A kettle will hold low and slow, roasting heat, or wide-open searing — if you start with the right amount of lit charcoal, make one small vent move, and then give the fire time to answer.

body.text: Start with the fire you want, not the fire you have to fight. Light only what the cook needs: a handful of lit briquettes, 6 to 10, for low and slow; 10 to 15 for the middle range; a quarter to half a chimney for roasting; a full chimney only when you mean searing. Dump a full chimney into a low-and-slow cook and then try to choke it down, and you'll get dirty smoke and a kettle that never settles.

Kelly's vent way: bottom dampers all the way open, always, and you adjust the heat with the top vent. Air comes in the bottom, feeds the fire, and leaves out the top, over the meat. Plenty of good kettle cooks run it the other way — top vent open, bottom vent doing the work — and that's fine too; both ends pull the same draw. Just pick one end to work and don't fight both at once.

One small move, then wait. A kettle answers slow — the charcoal, the metal, the air, and the food all have to catch up. Make one small vent move, wait 10 to 15 minutes, and watch the trend, not one reading. Moving the vent every two minutes makes bigger swings than the problem you started with.

Kelly doesn't cook by a dome thermometer. He reads the heat coming out the top vent, by hand. If you run a probe, clip it at the grate on the indirect side, near the food and not over the coals — the dome tells you what's happening up at the lid, not where the meat sits.

Set the fire up for the cook. A snake of unlit charcoal holds a long low cook; a pile or basket, the minion way, covers a moderate smoke; bank the coals to one side for two-zone roasting and searing, with the cool side as a safety zone if the food starts getting too dark. The unlit charcoal is what stretches a cook — it catches as the fire travels, so a long cook doesn't need a full chimney of lit coals to start.

Wind, lid, and ash will move your temperature on you. Wind pushing into the bottom vent runs the fire hotter, so turn the kettle so the vent isn't taking it head-on. Every lid lift feeds the fire oxygen — expect a dip as heat escapes, then a spike as the coals get more air. And ash choking the lower vents runs the fire cool, so clear it when it's safe to.

Treat temperatures as zones, not absolutes. A 225°F cook drifting between 225 and 250 is still fine; a 275°F cook wandering 260 to 290 is manageable. Steady matters more than a perfect number. And write the cook down — charcoal, vent, weather, result — in My Cooks, so the next cook doesn't start from scratch. That's what the app is for: a written-down memory for cooks.

takeaways: Light for the heat you want, not the heat you'll fight.
Bottom dampers wide open; adjust heat with the top vent.
One small vent move, then 10 to 15 minutes of patience.
Temperatures are zones; steady beats perfect.
Write the cook down in My Cooks.

title: Mistakes That Teach You the Pit
summary: Every good cook has served dry brisket, bitter bark, or ribs gone mushy. The pit teaches by pattern — read what went wrong, fix one thing, and cook again.

body.text: Cook to tenderness, not the clock. Time plans the day; it doesn't finish the meat. A brisket or a butt is done when the probe slides in tender; ribs are done when they bend and the surface cracks, not when the clock says so. Size, thickness, trim, pit temperature, weather, and wrapping all stretch or shorten a cook — so build in a buffer, and never let yourself end up slicing in a panic.

Dirty smoke is the bitter one. It comes from a smoldering, choked fire, wet or green wood, or just too much wood. Burn seasoned wood with clean airflow, and if the exhaust sits thick and white or gray for a long stretch, the meat is getting more bitter smoke than it needs. And don't fix a hot pit by shutting the vents until the fire suffocates — build a smaller fire instead. Choking the air trades heat for dirty smoke.

Match the wood to the meat. Strong smoke is great on beef, but it runs right over chicken, turkey, fish, and lighter pork. Poultry takes smoke fast, like cheese — a light hand, lighter woods like apple, cherry, peach, or pecan, don't keep feeding wood the whole cook, and cook it to a safe internal temperature.

Season for the size of the cut. A big brisket or butt needs enough salt and rub to carry through bark, fat, and interior — season all sides, edges, and seams, and let it go tacky before it hits the smoke. Thin cuts go the other way: too much rub, especially a salty or sugary one, turns pasty and buries the meat. And pulled pork and chopped brisket may want a little more seasoning after the cook, once it's mixed.

Trim with purpose. Thin flaps burn before the muscle gets tender. Thick hard fat blocks rub, smoke, and bark — a brisket cap wants about a quarter inch, a pork butt cap crosshatched or trimmed clean down to the meat. But don't scalp the cap off down to lean meat, or the heat gets straight at it. And find the grain before the bark forms, so slicing isn't a guessing game later.

Wrap by bark, not by number. Wrap when the bark is dark, set, and doesn't smear when you touch it — not because a thermometer hit a certain number. Wrap too early and you steam the bark soft; wait too long while the flat dries and the stall drags, and a wrap is what saves the cook. Paper protects bark better, foil is faster and wetter, and no wrap at all means the strongest bark and the longest cook.

Rest is part of the cook — the biggest tip of all. Slicing a brisket straight off the pit runs the juice onto the board and dries the flat. Rest it, and if it finishes early, hold it: foil, towels, and a cooler keep a brisket hot for hours, so finishing early beats finishing late. Ribs only need a brief settle before slicing. And slice brisket across the grain — the point's grain runs different from the flat, so rotate when you get to it.

Ribs should bite, not collapse. A good rib bites clean and pulls from the bone with a little resistance. If it falls apart when you pick it up, it went too far — usually too long wrapped. Sauce late, so it doesn't burn or go sticky in the wrong way.

Plan the eating time, then work backward. Long cooks need buffer for weather, stall, trim, wrap, and rest, and the sides ought to land with the meat, not after it. If the meat finishes early and you know how to hold it, that's a win, not a problem.

Write it down. This app exists because Kelly can't hold it all in his head, and most of us can't either. Meat weight, trim, rub, wood, pit temperature, wrap time, rest time, weather, and how it ate — one note in My Cooks turns a mistake into a lesson you don't repeat. And change one thing at a time, or you'll never know what fixed it.

takeaways: Cook to tenderness, not the clock.
Clean smoke beats heavy smoke.
Wrap by bark, not by number.
Rest is part of the cook — the biggest tip of all.
Change one thing at a time, and write it down in My Cooks.

title: Picking Your First Smoker
summary: There is no wrong first smoker — only the one that fits how you want to cook right now. Start with what you'll actually use, and let the skills grow from there.

body.text: The best first smoker is the one you'll actually use. Before you shop, ask three things: how much fire-tending do you want to do, how deep do you want the smoke, and what do you want to spend — in money and in upkeep. There is no wrong answer, only the one that fits how you cook right now.

Electric is the easiest way in. Plug it in, set the temperature, and let it run — steady heat, almost no babysitting, and it works where charcoal or open flames are restricted. The smoke runs light, and it can feel more like an oven with smoke. If easy is what gets you cooking, that's a good trade.
Gas is fast and familiar. It runs about like a gas grill, heats up quick, and keeps things simple. The smoke runs light to medium, it needs propane, and the cooking space is often smaller.

Pellet splits the difference. Push-button start, a digital controller holds the temperature, and real hardwood pellets give real — if milder — smoke. It costs more up front, and pellets keep costing. A lot of folks land here for the balance of ease and flavor.

Charcoal is the best teacher. Kettles and charcoal cabinets give you bold smoke, the cheapest way in, and they teach airflow, vent control, and fire management — skills that carry to any cooker you touch later. It takes practice, and there's ash to clean. Kelly started on a Weber kettle, and he'll tell you it makes beautiful, tasty barbecue. No fancy equipment needed. A barrel smoker, like the Weber Smokey Mountain, is a charcoal cabinet that stands upright, fire low and meat above, with a water pan in between. Some folks run water in it, some run it dry, especially on chicken. The water pan has a tendency to run the temperature lower, that's why you need to add hot water if you're using it. A lot of folks run the snake method in it too. It holds steady for hours with little fuss.

An offset — a stick burner — is the deepest smoke and the biggest capacity, and the most work. It wants constant fire-tending and wood splits, and it has the steepest learning curve. That's the long-term path if tradition is what you're chasing, not the easiest first step.

No cooker gatekeeping here. Pellet grills and gravity-fed charcoal smokers are fine if the cook's happy — charcoal and wood carry a lot of the flavor, but nobody should be bashed for their cooker. And starting simple doesn't lock you in. Plenty of good cooks end up with more than one pit as their skills and curiosity grow.

On money and upkeep, think in rough ranges: entry rigs around $150 to $350, mid-range pellet or bigger charcoal around $400 to $800, quality offsets and high-end pellet rigs $800 and up — but prices move, so shop the cooker, not the number. Electric and pellet rigs want routine cleaning and part checks; charcoal and offset rigs want ash and firebox care; gas rigs want burners and propane watched.

takeaways: The best first smoker is the one you'll actually use.
Charcoal teaches fire; electric and pellet teach ease.
No cooker gatekeeping — if the cook's happy, it's good barbecue.
Start simple. You can always add a second pit later.

title: Searing doesn't seal in the juices
summary: A good sear makes flavor, not a seal. Judge the cook by temperature, and rest it.

body.text: Plenty of folks swear a hard sear locks the juices in. It doesn't. Juices are water, and water doesn't stay put because the outside got brown. What a sear does is make flavor — that browned crust is where a lot of the taste lives.

That's why the reverse sear works so well. Cook it slow first, bring it up gentle to where you want it, then sear it hot at the end for the crust. You get the even cook and the crust both, instead of a gray band under a seared outside.

What actually keeps a cook juicy is pulling it at the right temperature and resting it. Resting is still cooking, and it's the biggest tip of all — give the juices time to settle back through the meat before you cut.

takeaways: Sear for flavor and crust, not for sealing.
Slow first, sear last — the reverse sear gets both.
Pull by temperature, then rest.

title: Don't soak your wood
summary: Wet chips don't make more smoke. They steam first, and the real smoke shows up late.

body.text: Soaking chips feels like it ought to help — more water, more smoke, right? It runs the other way. Wet wood has to boil its water off before it can smolder, so what you get first is steam, not smoke, and the real smoke shows up late.
Kelly doesn't soak chips in water at all. Dry wood makes clean smoke sooner, and chunks beat chips for a long cook anyway — chips flare and die fast, chunks smolder along.
Don't mix this up with the water pan. A water pan sits in the cooker to steady the heat; soaking chips just wets the fuel. Dry fuel, clean smoke, thin and blue.

takeaways: Wet wood steams before it smokes.
Dry chunks beat soaked chips for a long cook.
The water pan is not the same as soaking.

title: Cold meat takes the smoke better
summary: Straight from the fridge to the pit. The smoke works while the meat is still cool.

body.text: A lot of folks say meat needs to come to room temperature first. Kelly always likes his meat cold on the pit. Cold meat takes smoke better, because the smoke ring and the smoke flavor get to work while the meat is still cool — once the outside heats up past a point, that window closes.

An hour sitting on the counter doesn't change the cook much anyway. The middle of a brisket or a butt barely moves in that time, and you're just giving bacteria a head start. Fridge to pit is simpler and safer.
Judge it the way you always do: by temperature and by feel, not by the clock. Probe-tender beats a number, and rest is still the biggest tip.

takeaways: Fridge to pit — cold meat takes smoke better.
Room temperature is a wait that buys you nothing.
Pull by temperature and feel, then rest.

title: The bone doesn't flavor the meat
summary: Plenty of folks swear the bone seasons the meat. Meathead says it doesn't — and the argument is worth hearing out.

body.text: Ask around and plenty of good cooks will swear bone-in tastes better because the bone flavors the meat. Meathead's science says the bone itself doesn't season anything — flavor comes from the meat, the fat, the rub, and the smoke.

Bone-in cuts often do taste great, but that's usually because they get cooked gentler, trimmed less, and pulled at the right time — not because flavor leaked out of the bone. The bone can even slow the cook right next to it, since it shields that meat from the heat.

Kelly's rule covers the argument either way: if you're satisfied with your cook's taste and look, the comment section gets no vote. Cook bone-in or boneless, whichever makes you happy — that's what barbecue is all about.

takeaways: The bone doesn't season the meat — meat, fat, rub, and smoke do.
Bone-in tastes great for other reasons: gentler cooks, less trimming.
If you're happy with your cook, the argument is over.

body.text: Lump charcoal is just wood, charred and broken into chunks. Nothing added, so the smoke is pure wood smoke. It burns hotter than briquettes, which makes it good for searing and grilling. The trade-off is the pieces are all different sizes, so the fire is less even, and it burns through faster — on a long cook you may need to refuel.

Briquettes are ground charcoal pressed into uniform pillows, usually with a binder to hold the shape. Same size every time means a steady, even burn that lasts longer, which is why they're the pick for slow cooking — and for the snake method, where an even line of fuel is the whole trick. The trade-offs are more ash to clean up, and some brands use fillers that soften the smoke flavor.
Price is simple: lump costs more per bag, briquettes are the budget-friendly bag. Low ash on the lump side, easy clean-up; more ash on the briquette side, more cleaning.
Use what suits the cook. Hot and fast, reach for lump. Low and slow, reach for briquettes. Nobody's fire is wrong because of the bag they bought.

summary: Lump burns hotter and faster with pure wood smoke. Briquettes burn longer and steadier. Neither bag is wrong — pick the one that fits the cook.
takeaways: Lump: hotter, faster, pure wood smoke, pricier, low ash.
Briquettes: steadier, longer, budget-friendly, more ash.
Snake method wants uniform briquettes — an even line burns even.
title: Lump or briquettes? Both have a job
